items.prompt: Describe how a learner sets up a light microscope for a prepared slide of a leaf section so that a plan diagram can be made.
items.canonical_answer: First the lowest-power objective is swung into position and the slide is clipped to the stage with the section over the opening. Then, watching from the side, the objective is lowered close to the slide, and, looking through the eyepiece, the coarse focus is turned to move the objective away from the slide until the section appears, with the fine focus used to make it sharp and the light adjusted. The result is a sharp image at low power, where the whole section fits in the field of view, which is the power at which the plan diagram is made.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, taken in the order of the sequence: lowest-power objective in place and slide clipped to the stage (1); the objective lowered close to the slide while watched from the side, then focused by moving it away from the slide, coarse then fine (1); the light adjusted and the plan diagram made at low power, so that the whole section is in view, as the final outcome (1).
The steps must be in a workable order. Focusing by lowering the objective while looking through the eyepiece does not earn the second mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State one reason why the lowest-power objective is used first when a slide is put on the stage.
items.canonical_answer: It gives the widest field of view, so the specimen is easy to find, or it is the objective farthest from the slide, so there is little risk of the lens touching the glass.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one reason, either the widest field of view that makes the specimen easy to find or the greater distance of the lens from the slide that protects both. The reason must be stated, not just the instruction to start at low power.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: Describe how a thin piece of onion epidermis is stained and mounted on a slide for examination.
items.canonical_answer: First a drop of iodine solution is placed on a clean slide. Then the thin piece of epidermis, peeled with forceps, is laid flat in the drop. A coverslip is lowered at an angle onto it with a mounted needle, so that air is pushed out and no bubbles are trapped, and finally the excess liquid at the edge is soaked up with filter paper. The result is a thin, flat, stained layer under a coverslip.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, in order: a drop of stain, such as iodine solution, on a clean slide and the thin tissue laid flat in it (1); the coverslip lowered at an angle with a mounted needle (1); the result of that angle, no trapped air bubbles, or the excess liquid soaked up with filter paper as the final step (1).
A thick or folded piece of tissue, or a coverslip dropped flat, does not earn its mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State the reason why a coverslip is lowered at an angle with a mounted needle and not dropped flat onto the specimen.
items.canonical_answer: It avoids trapping air bubbles, which appear as round dark-edged shapes and hide the cells.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, that air bubbles are not trapped because the air is pushed out ahead of the advancing edge, or that bubbles hide the specimen.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by calibrating an eyepiece graticule.
items.canonical_answer: Working out the length that one graticule division stands for, in micrometres, for one objective lens, by comparing the graticule with the scale of known length on a stage micrometer.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words are the length of one graticule division and the comparison with a scale of known length, the stage micrometer. A statement that gives the calibration as measuring cells does not earn the mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: On one microscope, 50 eyepiece graticule divisions line up exactly with 0.40 mm of the scale on the stage micrometer. Calculate the length in micrometres of one graticule division, showing the working.
items.canonical_answer: Equation: length of one division = length on the stage micrometer in µm ÷ number of graticule divisions. Conversion: 0.40 × 1000 = 400 µm. Substitution: 400 ÷ 50 = 8 µm. One graticule division is 8 µm.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the conversion of 0.40 mm to 400 µm with the equation or substitution step (1); the final answer of 8 µm with its unit (1).
An answer of 0.008 with no unit, or of 8 mm, loses the answer mark. A correct answer with no working earns both marks only where the working is plainly implied by the answer.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: On one microscope, 30 eyepiece graticule divisions line up exactly with 12 divisions of a stage micrometer. Each division of the stage micrometer is 0.01 mm. Calculate the length in micrometres of one graticule division, showing the working.
items.canonical_answer: Length on the micrometer: 12 × 0.01 = 0.12 mm. Conversion: 0.12 × 1000 = 120 µm. Substitution: 120 ÷ 30 = 4 µm. One graticule division is 4 µm.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the length on the micrometer converted to micrometres, 120 µm, as the working step (1); the final answer of 4 µm with its unit (1).
Dividing 12 by 30 without converting the length gives 0.4, which is not an answer in micrometres and loses the answer mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A learner calibrates a graticule with the ×10 objective and finds that one division is 10 µm. The learner changes to the ×40 objective, leaves the stage micrometer out and measures a cell that spans 6 divisions, giving its length as 60 µm. Explain why this length is wrong and what the learner should have done.
items.canonical_answer: The value of 10 µm per division belongs to the ×10 objective only. In this case the ×40 objective enlarges the specimen more, so the cell spans more divisions and each division stands for a shorter length, so 60 µm is not its length. The learner should have calibrated the graticule again for the ×40 objective, with the stage micrometer, before measuring.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the reason, because a calibration holds for one objective and a higher-power objective makes each division stand for a shorter length (1); the correction, that the graticule is calibrated again with the stage micrometer at ×40 before the cell is measured (1).
The answer must refer to the case given. A general statement that calibration matters earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the mean when the sizes of several cells are measured.
items.canonical_answer: The total of the measurements divided by the number of cells measured.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words are the total of the measurements and the number of measurements as the divisor. A statement that the mean is the middle or the most common value does not earn the mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: At the ×40 objective, one eyepiece graticule division is 2.5 µm. The widths of six epidermal cells, measured across the same direction, are 10, 12, 11, 9, 13 and 11 divisions. Calculate the mean width of the cells in micrometres, showing the working.
items.canonical_answer: Total: 10 + 12 + 11 + 9 + 13 + 11 = 66 divisions. Mean in divisions: 66 ÷ 6 = 11 divisions. Actual size: 11 × 2.5 = 27.5 µm. The mean width is 27.5 µm.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the mean in divisions from the total and the number of cells, 11 divisions, as the working (1); the answer 27.5 µm after the calibration is applied, with its unit (1).
An answer of 11 with no unit, or of 27.5 mm, loses the answer mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: One eyepiece graticule division is 4 µm at the objective in use. The lengths of four guard cells are 7, 8, 6 and 7 divisions. Calculate the mean length of the guard cells in micrometres, showing the working.
items.canonical_answer: Total: 7 + 8 + 6 + 7 = 28 divisions. Mean in divisions: 28 ÷ 4 = 7 divisions. Actual size: 7 × 4 = 28 µm. The mean length is 28 µm.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the total divided by 4 to give the mean in divisions, 7, as the working (1); the answer 28 µm with its unit (1).
Four values are needed in the mean, so a division by 3 or by 28 does not earn the working mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A learner measures one epidermal cell on a slide and reports its length as 28 µm. The other five cells measured by a classmate on the same slide are between 30 and 36 µm. Explain why the classmate's mean of several cells is a better guide to the cell length than the one measurement of the learner.
items.canonical_answer: In this case the learner's cell is shorter than all five of the others, so one cell can mislead because cells in one tissue differ in size. The mean of several cells is a better guide because an unusually short or long cell has less effect on a total shared among many cells, so it represents the tissue better.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the reason that cells differ, so one cell may be unusual, as shown by this cell being shorter than the other five (1); the reason that the mean of several cells reduces the effect of an unusual cell and so is more representative (1).
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A learner finds that 25 eyepiece graticule divisions line up with 0.30 mm on the stage micrometer. The learner writes 0.30 mm = 30 µm and says that one division is 30 ÷ 25 = 1.2 µm. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a mistake in converting millimetres to micrometres: 30 is 0.30 divided by 10, not 0.30 × 1000. In fact 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.30 × 1000 = 300 µm, and 300 ÷ 25 = 12 µm for one division. The test is to work a small case through: 0.7 mm is 0.7 × 1000 = 700 µm, not 7 µm, so the learner's value is ten times too small.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the millimetres were converted wrongly, by dividing by 10 instead of multiplying by 1000 (1); the correct idea or the test, that 0.30 mm is 300 µm and one division is 12 µm (1).
The card is a discrimination between a correct and a wrong conversion, not a repeat of the calibration method. The value 12 µm without a reason earns the second mark only with the 300 µm step.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by sampling when the number of cells on a slide is estimated.
items.canonical_answer: Counting the cells in a few chosen fields of view or grid squares, found at random, and using the mean count to estimate the number on the whole slide.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words are counting in a few fields or squares and using the mean to estimate for the whole slide. A statement that every cell is counted does not earn the mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A grid has squares each 1 mm by 1 mm. The numbers of cells counted in five squares chosen at random are 34, 29, 31, 36 and 30. Calculate the mean number of cells per square, and state it as a count per mm², showing the working.
items.canonical_answer: Total: 34 + 29 + 31 + 36 + 30 = 160 cells. Mean per square: 160 ÷ 5 = 32 cells. Each square has an area of 1 mm², so the count per area is 32 ÷ 1 = 32 cells per mm².
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the total divided by 5, with the working (1); the answer of 32 cells per mm² with its unit (1).
An answer of 32 with no unit loses the answer mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A mean of 18 cells is counted per field of view on a slide. The specimen is large enough that 150 fields of view are needed to cover it. Calculate an estimate of the number of cells in the specimen, showing the working.
items.canonical_answer: Equation: estimate = mean number per field × number of fields. Substitution: 18 × 150 = 2700 cells. The estimate is 2700 cells.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the equation or substitution of the mean and the number of fields (1); the answer of 2700 cells, as a result of the multiplication, with its unit (1).
A value of 168, from adding the two numbers, does not earn the working mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A student counts the cells in one field of view at the centre of a crowded slide and multiplies the count by the number of fields on the slide. Explain why this estimate of the number of cells is unreliable, and how the sample could be improved.
items.canonical_answer: In this case the estimate is unreliable because cells are seldom spread evenly and a crowded centre field holds more cells than a typical field, so the estimate is too high. The sample is improved by counting several fields chosen at random and using the mean, so that crowded and sparse fields are both included.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the reason, that the cells are not spread evenly and this one field is not typical of the slide (1); the improvement, several fields chosen at random and the mean found, because this includes crowded and sparse fields (1).
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State one feature of a plan diagram.
items.canonical_answer: It shows the outlines of the tissue layers in correct proportion, with no individual cells drawn.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature, either that the tissue layers are drawn in correct proportion to their thickness in the specimen or that no individual cells are drawn. Cell outlines in the drawing are not a feature of a plan diagram.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A leaf section has an upper epidermis 20 µm thick, a palisade layer 80 µm thick, a spongy layer 100 µm thick and a lower epidermis 20 µm thick. The student draws a plan diagram 110 mm tall from surface to surface. Explain how thick each layer should be drawn, and why no cells are drawn.
items.canonical_answer: In this case the whole section is 20 + 80 + 100 + 20 = 220 µm, and 110 mm for 220 µm is 0.5 mm for each µm, so each layer is drawn in the same proportion: 20 × 0.5 = 10 mm, 80 × 0.5 = 40 mm, 100 × 0.5 = 50 mm and 20 × 0.5 = 10 mm. No cells are drawn because a plan diagram shows the distribution of the tissues alone, so the drawing is of the layers.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the thicknesses drawn, 10 mm, 40 mm, 50 mm and 10 mm, found with one factor for each layer (1); the reason, because a plan diagram shows the layout of tissues and not cells (1).
The data given in this case are used, so if one layer is wrong the proportion mark is not given.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A learner is asked to make a plan diagram of a section of a stem. The learner draws every cell in the xylem and the cortex as a small circle and says that more detail makes a better plan diagram. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to confuse a plan diagram with a drawing of cells. In fact a plan diagram shows the outlines and layout of the tissues alone, in correct proportion, and the cells are drawn in a high-power cell drawing. The test is to ask whether the drawing shows cell outlines or only tissue regions: the learner's drawing shows cell outlines, so it is not a plan diagram.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that individual cells were drawn in a plan diagram (1); the correct idea or the test, that a plan diagram shows tissue regions only, with cells left for the high-power drawing (1).
The card is a discrimination between two sets of drawing, not a repeat of the definition of a plan diagram.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State one feature of the way a plant cell wall is drawn in a cell drawing made at high power.
items.canonical_answer: It is drawn as two lines, to show the thickness of the wall, and not as a single line.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature, that the wall is drawn as two lines with a gap between them. A single line, or a thick line, does not earn the mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A learner looks at onion epidermal cells at ×400 and sees rectangular cells with thick walls, a small stained nucleus near each wall and a large clear central vacuole. The drawing shows a nucleus as large as half of each cell, with mitochondria drawn as ovals with folded inner membranes copied from a textbook. Explain two errors in the drawing.
items.canonical_answer: In this case the nucleus is drawn too large, because it is a small part of the cell and the drawing must show the relative sizes of the parts. The mitochondria with folded membranes are not observable at ×400 with a light microscope, so they were copied from a book, and a cell drawing includes only the features that can be seen.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the nucleus drawn at the wrong relative size, as the specimen shows a small nucleus (1); the mitochondria drawn although they cannot be seen at this magnification, because only observable features are drawn (1).
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by an observable feature of a specimen.
items.canonical_answer: A feature that can be seen in the specimen, slide or photomicrograph at the magnification used, such as shape, size, the presence of a wall or the thickness of a layer.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words are can be seen, in the specimen or image, as opposed to being known from books or inferred. A statement of what a structure does is not a definition.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State one difference between an observable feature and an interpretation of it.
items.canonical_answer: An observable feature is something that can be seen, such as the cells containing small green structures, whereas an interpretation is a statement from knowledge, such as that the cells carry out photosynthesis.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one difference, the contrast between what can be seen and what is inferred from knowledge, with a matching example or a clear statement of each. A pair of examples that are both observations earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State one feature of the lines in a clear biological drawing.
items.canonical_answer: The lines are sharp and unbroken, drawn once in a sharp pencil, with no shading.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature of the lines, either sharp, or unbroken and single, or not shaded. A feature of the label lines or of the size of the drawing is not a feature of the lines of the drawing.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A learner makes a cell drawing 20 mm wide in the corner of a space 120 mm by 150 mm. The lines are sketchy, with several lines drawn over each other, and the nucleus is shaded with pencil dots. Explain two changes that would make the drawing clearer.
items.canonical_answer: In this case the drawing should be made larger so that it uses most of the space available, because a small drawing cannot show shapes and details clearly. The sketchy lines should be single, sharp, unbroken lines and the shading should be removed, because shading hides the structure beneath it.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the drawing enlarged to use most of the space, with the reason that details are clearer (1); sharp, unbroken single lines, or the shading removed, because shading hides the structure (1). The answer refers to the situation given, a drawing 20 mm wide in a large space.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by showing the working in a calculation.
items.canonical_answer: Writing down each step, the equation, the conversion of units, the substitution of values and the answer with its unit, so that each step can be checked and credited.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words are writing out the steps, such as the equation and the substitution, so that they can be checked. Giving only the final answer is not showing the working.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A drawing of a palisade cell is 56 mm long. The length of the cell measured with a calibrated graticule is 70 µm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing, showing the working.
items.canonical_answer: Equation: magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Conversion: 56 × 1000 = 56 000 µm. Substitution: 56 000 ÷ 70 = 800. The magnification is ×800.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the equation with both lengths in the same unit, 56 000 µm, as the working (1); the answer ×800 (1).
The division 56 ÷ 70 = 0.8 without the conversion earns no answer mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: In a leaf section the palisade layer is 90 µm thick and the spongy layer is 150 µm thick. Calculate the ratio of the thickness of the palisade layer to that of the spongy layer in its simplest whole-number form, showing the working.
items.canonical_answer: The ratio is 90 : 150. Dividing both numbers by 30 gives 90 ÷ 30 = 3 and 150 ÷ 30 = 5. The ratio is 3 : 5.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the ratio written as 90 : 150 and divided by a common number as the working (1); the simplest form, 3 : 5 (1).

A ratio of 0.6 with no second number, or one that can be reduced further such as 9 : 15, does not earn the answer mark. A ratio of two lengths in the same unit has no unit of its own, so the answer mark is for the simplest whole-number form.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A cell is 24 mm long on a photomicrograph taken at ×400. A learner writes 24 ÷ 400 = 0.06 and gives the actual length as 0.06 µm. Explain why the answer is wrong and state the correct length.
items.canonical_answer: In this case the division 24 ÷ 400 = 0.06 is in millimetres, because the image size was in millimetres, so the unit µm was wrong. Converting gives 0.06 × 1000 = 60 µm, so the cell is 60 µm long.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the reason, that the answer of the division is in millimetres because the image size is in millimetres, so the unit was wrong (1); the correct length 60 µm, from the conversion (1). The case given is a photomicrograph, so the unit follows from the image size.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a photomicrograph.
items.canonical_answer: A photograph of a specimen taken through a light microscope.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words are a photograph and taken through a light microscope. A drawing made from the microscope is not a photomicrograph.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State one difference between examining a slide under the microscope and examining a photomicrograph of the specimen.
items.canonical_answer: A slide can be refocused and measured against a calibrated graticule, whereas a photomicrograph is a fixed image at one focus that is measured with a ruler and the magnification.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one difference, either the slide can be refocused through its thickness or the light adjusted whereas the photomicrograph is fixed, or the slide is measured with a graticule whereas the photomicrograph is measured with a ruler and the magnification.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by an adaptation of an organism to its habitat.
items.canonical_answer: A feature of the structure of an organism that helps it to survive and reproduce in its habitat.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words are a feature of structure and helps survival or reproduction in its habitat. A change made by one individual in its lifetime is not the meaning.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A section of a leaf from a plant on a dry, rocky hillside shows a waxy cuticle 8 µm thick on the outside of the upper epidermis. Explain how this feature helps the plant to survive in a dry habitat.
items.canonical_answer: Wax is waterproof, which means that less water evaporates through the surface of the leaf, so the plant loses water more slowly, which helps it survive where water is scarce.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: how the feature works, that the wax waterproofs the surface so that less water evaporates from it (1); the consequence for survival, that the plant loses less water where water is scarce (1).
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt: A section of a floating water lily leaf is 260 µm thick, of which the spongy layer is 170 µm, and it has large air spaces between the cells. Explain how the air spaces suit this leaf to its habitat.
items.canonical_answer: In this case the large air spaces are filled with air, so the leaf is buoyant and floats at the surface in the light, and the spaces also let gases diffuse through the leaf because they connect the cells. This is a tendency that suits a leaf floating on a pond.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the buoyancy reason, that air in the spaces makes the leaf float at the surface (1); the second reason, that the air spaces let gases move through the leaf, linked to the specimen given, because the spaces connect the cells (1).
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt:
A student calibrates the eyepiece graticule of a light microscope and then measures cells from the inner surface of an onion bulb scale. The stage micrometer scale is 1.00 mm long, divided into 100 divisions of 0.01 mm each. The graticule has 100 divisions. All the values below are our own invented readings, not taken from any published source.

Table 1 Calibration of the graticule

| Objective | Graticule divisions that line up | Stage micrometer divisions that line up |
|---|---|---|
| ×10 | 50 | 50 |
| ×40 | 100 | 25 |

With the ×10 objective the student then measures the length of eight cells along the same direction.

Table 2 Lengths of eight onion cells at ×10

| Cell | Length of cell / graticule divisions |
|---|---|
| 1 | 28 |
| 2 | 31 |
| 3 | 27 |
| 4 | 30 |
| 5 | 32 |
| 6 | 29 |
| 7 | 30 |
| 8 | 33 |

(a) Calculate the length in µm of one graticule division at ×10, showing the working. [2]
(b) Calculate the mean length of the cells in µm, showing each step. [3]
(c) Calculate the length in µm of one graticule division at ×40, and explain why it differs from your answer to (a). [2]
(d) State one source of error in reading a cell length against the graticule, and state the uncertainty in µm of one reading at ×10 if the reading can be wrong by one division. [1]
(e) Suggest one improvement that would make the mean length more reliable, and state the reason. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Length on the micrometer: 50 × 0.01 = 0.50 mm. Conversion: 0.50 × 1000 = 500 µm. Substitution: 500 ÷ 50 = 10 µm. One division is 10 µm at ×10.
(b) Total: 28 + 31 + 27 + 30 + 32 + 29 + 30 + 33 = 240 divisions. Mean in divisions: 240 ÷ 8 = 30 divisions. Actual size: 30 × 10 = 300 µm. The mean length is 300 µm.
(c) Length on the micrometer: 25 × 0.01 = 0.25 mm. Conversion: 0.25 × 1000 = 250 µm. Substitution: 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5 µm. One division is 2.5 µm at ×40. It differs because the ×40 objective enlarges the specimen more, so the same length spans more divisions and each division stands for a shorter length.
(d) The ends of a cell are blurred or fall between two divisions, so the reading is to the nearest division. The uncertainty of one reading is 10 µm at ×10.
(e) Measure more cells, for example 20, because the mean is then less affected by one unusually long or short cell.
marking_guidance: Table and headings: Table 1 and Table 2 give the quantity and unit in each column heading and the body holds values alone, so the readings are taken from them.

Part (a), 2 marks: the length on the micrometer converted to 500 µm as working (1); the answer 10 µm with its unit (1). Part (b), 3 marks: the total of 240 divisions (1); the mean of 30 divisions from dividing by 8 (1); the conversion to 300 µm with its unit (1).

Part (c), 2 marks: the value 2.5 µm with working (1); the reason, that the higher-power objective makes each division stand for a shorter length (1). Part (d), 1 mark: a source of error, such as cell ends falling between divisions, with the uncertainty of 10 µm (a reading error of one division).

Part (e), 2 marks: an improvement, more cells measured, a larger sample or a repeat on another slide (1); the reason, that the mean is less affected by an unusual cell, so the conclusion is more reliable (1). Taking more care is not an improvement, and a scale error from a poor calibration at ×40 does not belong to a mean at ×10.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 4.2 from its claim ledger. Scenarios and measurements are our own and unverified.

items.prompt:
A student compares transverse sections of two leaves with a light microscope at ×10, where one graticule division was calibrated as 10 µm. Specimen A is from a plant growing on a dry, rocky hillside. Specimen B is a floating leaf of a water lily from a pond. The student measured the tissue layers with the graticule. All values are our own invented measurements, not taken from any published source.

Table 3 Thickness of the tissue layers

| Tissue layer | Specimen A thickness / µm | Specimen B thickness / µm |
|---|---|---|
| Upper epidermis | 50 | 20 |
| Palisade layer | 140 | 60 |
| Spongy layer | 120 | 170 |
| Lower epidermis | 30 | 10 |
| Whole section | 340 | 260 |

In the section of A a clear waxy layer about 8 µm thick covers the upper epidermis, the spongy layer has small air spaces, and stomata are seen mainly in the lower epidermis. In the section of B the waxy layer is too thin to measure, the spongy layer has very large air spaces between its cells, and stomata are seen in the upper epidermis only.

(a) Describe what a plan diagram of Specimen A would show and what it would not show. [2]
(b) The plan diagram of Specimen A is to be 68 mm tall from the upper surface to the lower surface. Calculate the magnification of the drawing and the thickness at which the palisade layer should be drawn, in mm, showing the working. [3]
(c) Compare Specimen A and Specimen B using two observable features, with values where Table 3 gives them. [2]
(d) Explain how one observed feature of Specimen B suits a floating leaf. [2]
(e) Suggest one improvement that would make the comparison of the two habitats more reliable. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The plan diagram would show the outlines of the four tissue layers, upper epidermis, palisade layer, spongy layer and lower epidermis, drawn in correct proportion to their thickness in the section. It would not show any individual cells.
(b) The drawing height in micrometres is 68 × 1000 = 68 000 µm. Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 68 000 ÷ 340 = 200, so the drawing is ×200. The palisade layer is 140 × 200 = 28 000 µm, which is 28 mm.
(c) Any two comparisons of observable features, such as: the palisade layer in A is thicker (140 µm) whereas in B it is 60 µm; the spongy layer in B is thicker (170 µm) than in A (120 µm) and has very large air spaces whereas A has small ones; the whole section of A is thicker (340 µm) whereas B is 260 µm; A has a waxy layer about 8 µm thick whereas B has one too thin to measure; stomata are mainly in the lower epidermis of A whereas B has them in the upper epidermis only.
(d) The very large air spaces in the spongy layer are filled with air, so the leaf is buoyant and floats at the surface, and the air spaces also let gases diffuse through the leaf. Stomata only in the upper epidermis suit it because the upper surface is the one in the air, so gases can enter there.
(e) Measure the layers in sections of several leaves of each plant, because thickness varies from place to place and between leaves, so the comparison is less affected by one unusual section.
marking_guidance: Table and headings: Table 3 has the quantity and unit in each column heading, and its values are ours, so the comparison is made from them.

Part (a), 2 marks: the outlines of the tissue layers in correct proportion (1); no individual cells drawn (1). Part (b), 3 marks: the conversion of 68 mm to 68 000 µm (1); the magnification of ×200 from the equation magnification = image size ÷ actual size (1); the palisade layer 28 mm with its unit (1). The scale is the same for every layer, so 10 mm, 28 mm, 24 mm and 6 mm are drawn.

Part (c), 2 marks: two comparisons, each naming one feature in both specimens with a value or a description (1 each). A comparison that states a function, such as A is better at saving water, is an interpretation and is not credited as an observable feature.

Part (d), 2 marks: the feature linked to how it works, air spaces make the leaf buoyant or let gases diffuse (1); the link to the habitat, floating at the surface, or stomata in the surface in the air (1). Part (e), 1 mark: an improvement, such as more sections or leaves for each plant, with the reason that one section may be unusual, so a limitation of one section is removed and the conclusion is more reliable.
